displayQuote: History is more or less bunk

meta.title: Who really said "History is more or less bunk"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Henry Ford really said it — printed in the Chicago Tribune of 25 May 1916, interviewed by Charles N. Wheeler. But he said "more or less bunk," not "History is bunk."
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'History is more or less bunk'?
meta.ogDescription: Yes, Henry Ford said it — Chicago Tribune, 25 May 1916. The famous three-word version 'History is bunk' is the newspapers' compression of his actual words.

answer.label: Spoken by
answer.authorDates: 1863–1947 · American industrialist, founder of the Ford Motor Company
answer.sourceLine: Ford said it to Chicago Tribune reporter Charles N. Wheeler, in an interview the paper printed on 25 May 1916 — and he owned the word “bunk” under oath at his 1919 libel trial. The wording is genuine; what is not genuine is the three-word slogan “History is bunk,” which is the newspapers’ compression of it.

source.heading: Where it comes from

docMeta.dd: “Fight to Disarm His Life and Work, Henry Ford Vows”

source.excerpt: I don’t know whether Napoleon did or did not try to get across there and I don’t care. I don’t know much about history, and I wouldn’t give a nickel for all the history in the world. It means nothing to me. History is more or less bunk. It’s tradition. We don’t want tradition. We want to live in the present and the only history that is worth a tinker’s damn is the history we make today.
trail: Wikiquote ↗ carries the line in its sourced section — not among its disputed or misattributed entries — printing the fuller passage and citing an interview in the Chicago Tribune of 25 May 1916.

P. Watt’s peer-reviewed article “Debunking Ford’s relation to the past” ↗ (Journal of Management History, 2021) identifies the source as the fourth and final instalment of a weekly Tribune series of interviews conducted by Charles Wheeler, and cites it in its bibliography as “Fight to disarm his life and work, Henry Ford Vows,” Chicago Tribune, 25th May 1916.

The Henry Ford ↗ — the museum Ford founded — states that the Tribune quoted him saying “history is more or less bunk,” and that at the Mt. Clemens trial he replied “I did not say it was bunk. It was bunk to me…”
The phrase-origin reference phrases.org.uk ↗ independently gives the same fuller quotation and attributes it to the Chicago Tribune in 1916, though without the exact date or the reporter’s name.
source.excerptNote: Transcriptions of this passage differ slightly. Wikiquote gives the text above; the Journal of Management History quotes the same interview with “a tinker’s dam” and carries it further: “That’s the trouble with the world. We’re living in books and history and tradition. We want to get away from that and take care of today.”
source.rightsNote: The words were first published in the Chicago Tribune of 25 May 1916. Works published in the United States before 1931 are in the public domain, so both the short line and the fuller passage may be quoted freely.

author.metaLine: 1863–1947 · American industrialist & founder of the Ford Motor Company
author.bio: Henry Ford (1863–1947) founded the Ford Motor Company and pioneered the moving assembly line and the mass-produced, affordable automobile — the system that came to be called Fordism. He was also one of the most talked-about men alive: his Five-Dollar Day, his campaign against American entry into the First World War, and later his antisemitic publishing all kept him in the headlines. The same man who dismissed book history went on to build Greenfield Village, an outdoor museum of almost a hundred relocated historic buildings, to tell the story his own way.

misattribution.heading: The name is right. The wording usually isn’t.
misattribution.intro: This is the rare famous quote where the attribution holds up and the wording is what went wrong. Three things get mangled.

items.why: The three-word slogan is the version everyone repeats, but it is not what the Tribune printed. Scholarship following Roger Butterfield’s 1965 essay records that headline writers and editorialists reduced “history is more or less bunk” to the pithy three-word paraphrase, which then became fixed in Ford legend ↗. Confusingly, Ford himself later used the bare form — Wikiquote cites an October 1921 New York Times piece headlined “History is Bunk, Says Henry Ford” ↗.

Transcriptions of the same 1916 interview differ on this word: Wikiquote prints “a tinker’s damn” ↗, while the Journal of Management History quotation of the same passage reads “a tinker’s dam” ↗. Neither spelling changes the sense.

The remark is often placed at Ford’s libel trial, because that is when it went national. In fact it was printed three years earlier, in the 1916 Tribune interview; the trial is where defence attorneys questioned him about it ↗ and the story exploded.

On the stand Ford narrowed the claim rather than repeating it: “I did not say it was bunk. It was bunk to me” ↗. What he rejected was the schoolbook history of kings and generals — not the past itself, as the museum and village he went on to build make plain.

misattribution.truthLine: Ford did say it, and the record is clean: the Chicago Tribune printed it on 25 May 1916 ↗. He just said “more or less bunk” — and the qualifier is the whole argument.

context.heading: Why a throwaway line became a national catchphrase
lead: Ford said it in the middle of a fight about war. In 1916 he was the country’s loudest opponent of the American preparedness movement, and the Chicago Tribune answered with an editorial headlined “Ford Is an Anarchist.” Ford sued for libel. When the case came to trial in 1919 at Mt. Clemens, Michigan, the argument had drifted from whether he was an anarchist to whether he was an ignorant man — so the defence put him on the stand and quizzed him about history. That cross-examination is what pulled a line buried in a 1916 interview onto front pages across the country. Ford technically won: the jury awarded him six cents in damages ↗ against the million dollars he had asked for.

What he actually meant was narrower than the slogan suggests. Ford was not rejecting the past; he was rejecting the schoolbook version of it — kings, generals, dates to be memorised — in favour of the tools and work of ordinary people. In his 1922 book My Life and Work he put the same thought positively: “An educated man is not one whose memory is trained to carry a few dates in history – he is one who can accomplish things” ↗.
context.detailsSummary: Ford’s own gloss — and the museum he built to answer the charge
detailsBody: Scholarship records that the humiliation of the witness stand is precisely what launched Ford’s career as a collector. He told his secretary Ernst G. Liebold he was going to “give the people an idea of real history” and start a museum showing “just what actually happened in years gone by” — a plan Liebold explicitly connected to the trial (Watt, Journal of Management History, 2021 ↗).

Speaking about Greenfield Village in 1935, Ford drew the line himself: “What they call history IS bunk. Once I went to history books to find out what kind of a harrow people used to cultivate their land. Couldn’t find it. Nothing but kings and battles. That is the kind of history I think is bunk. The real story of humanity is how the people lived and grew” (quoted in Watt, 2021 ↗).
The Edison Institute — the museum complex beside Greenfield Village — opened on 21 October 1929 ↗, dedicated to Thomas Edison at the “Light’s Golden Jubilee” celebration.
